title: What competence rules apply to statutory functions at NSW mines?
description: How NSW practising certificates for mine statutory functions work, the 5 year maintenance of competence hours from 1 October 2025, audits and renewal.
shortAnswer: In New South Wales, a person exercising a statutory function at a mine, such as mining engineering manager, undermanager, deputy, open cut examiner, electrical engineer or quarry manager, must hold a current practising certificate issued by the NSW Resources Regulator under Schedule 10 of the Work Health and Safety (Mines and Petroleum Sites) Regulation 2022. Certificates last up to 5 years and carry a mandatory maintenance of competence condition of 60 to 120 learning hours per certificate period.
keyTakeaways: Holding a practising certificate became mandatory from October 1, 2020 for statutory functions that require one, after a staged transition that began in 2017.
Every certificate is issued for up to 5 years with a condition to maintain competence under a scheme gazetted by the Regulator, and to keep contact details current.

Under the scheme gazetted from October 1, 2025, total learning ranges from 60 hours (for example deputy, open cut examiner, underground mine supervisor) to 120 hours (engineering managers), split across three learning groups.

First-time holders must complete the Regulator's Learning from Disasters program or at least 7 hours of formal learning on disaster topics, and no more than 40% of hours can be claimed in any one year.
The Regulator audits holders randomly each year using external auditors, and practising in a statutory function on an expired certificate is an offense.
regulator: NSW Resources Regulator, Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development
appliesTo: Individuals exercising statutory functions at NSW coal mines, underground mines and quarries, including mining, electrical and mechanical engineering managers, undermanagers, deputies, ventilation officers and auditors, open cut examiners, underground mine supervisors, electrical and mechanical engineers, and quarry managers
Mine operators that nominate and rely on statutory function holders
Training providers delivering formal learning recognized under the maintenance of competence scheme

sections.heading: What is a practising certificate and who needs one?

blocks.text: A practising certificate is the NSW Resources Regulator's authorization for an individual to exercise a specified statutory function at a mine. The Regulator's [practising certificates overview](https://www.resources.nsw.gov.au/resources-regulator/safety/certification/practising-certificates/practising-certificates-overview) states that "an individual must hold a current practising certificate to practise in the statutory function", and that certificates specify the function under Schedule 10 of the Work Health and Safety (Mines and Petroleum Sites) Regulation 2022.

To be eligible, an applicant must hold a valid certificate of competence or qualifications for the function, or rely on mutual recognition of an equivalent certificate from another state or New Zealand. Quarry manager tier 2 applicants must also show relevant practical experience and complete required units in emergency preparedness and response.

The certificate of competence and the practising certificate do different jobs. The certificate of competence proves the person met the entry standard, often through examination. The practising certificate is time limited and conditional, so it tests whether the person has kept their knowledge current. That distinction mirrors the difference between [completion tracking and competency verification](/compare/completion-tracking-vs-competency-verification).

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects NSW Resources Regulator guidance as at November 2026, including the maintenance of competence scheme gazetted from October 1, 2025 and the Regulator's revised scheme guide (version 2.0, April 2026). The gazetted notice is the binding requirement. Check the Regulator's pages before relying on any hour figure.

sections.heading: When did practising certificates become mandatory?

blocks.text: Practising certificates became mandatory on October 1, 2020 for those exercising statutory functions that require one. The Regulator phased them in by function between 2017 and 2020: engineering managers first, with an invitation period from September 1, 2017, followed by undermanagers and quarry managers, then ventilation, dust explosion, open cut examiner and engineer roles, and finally deputies and underground mine supervisors.

The Regulator's [revised scheme guide](https://www.resources.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-09/guide-new-moc-scheme-from-1-Oct-2025.pdf) explains that maintenance of competence was developed in 2017 following recommendations from inquiries into the Moura No. 2 and Pike River mining disasters, which highlighted competency gaps in mine management. An evaluation in 2023 led to the simplified scheme that applies to certificates granted for periods from October 1, 2025.

sections.heading: How many maintenance of competence hours are required?

blocks.text: Total learning over the 5 year certificate period ranges from 60 to 120 hours, depending on the statutory function. The Regulator's guide says hours increase with the level of supervision or management and with the risk of the mine type, from surface mines to underground coal mines.

blocks.text: Group 1 covers mining and WHS systems and group 2 covers WHS legislation, emergency management and leadership, each with a minimum of 33% of hours. Group 3, general WHS, is capped at 33%. Holders of a quarry manager certificate restricted to a named quarry are exempt from the hours until they upgrade, and tier 3 quarries do not require a practising certificate holder.

sections.heading: What changed in the scheme from October 1, 2025?

blocks.text: The 2025 scheme keeps the three groups but removes most of the proportion rules that made logging complex. The Regulator's [fact sheet on the changes](https://www.resources.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-09/fact-sheet-changes-to-moc-ps-from-1-Oct-25.pdf) lists the main differences from the scheme in place since September 1, 2017:

items: **Annual spread:** up to 40% of total hours can be claimed in any one year, up from a 33% maximum.

**Formal learning:** the minimum formal learning proportions by level (66% for higher managers, 50% for middle managers, 33% for supervisors) were removed, along with the 50% cap on most formal types.
**Informal learning:** expanded from 14 to 19 recognized types, with most caps changed from 4 hours a year to 20 hours over 5 years.
**Learning from Disasters:** 7 hours of formal disaster learning is mandatory for all first-time holders and optional for continuing holders who have already done it.

**Transition:** holders with certificates in force at October 1, 2025 can choose which scheme their current and previous logs comply with; new certificates for periods from that date must use the new scheme.

blocks.text: Excess hours cannot be carried over between renewal periods. The guide's worked example shows a deputy completing 60 hours as 24, 0, 24, 0 and 12 hours across the five years, which respects the 40% annual limit.

sections.heading: How are holders audited, and what happens at renewal?

blocks.text: The Regulator audits certificate holders randomly each year, using external organizations contracted for the purpose, and reports the outcomes of each financial year's audit program to the NSW Mining and Petroleum Competence Board. Selected holders must produce their logbook and supporting evidence such as certificates and attendance records.

According to the Regulator's [renewal guidance](https://www.resources.nsw.gov.au/resources-regulator/safety/certification/practising-certificates/renew-vary-or-revoke), a holder can apply to renew once the certificate is within 6 months of expiry, the process can take up to 6 weeks, and the application includes a declaration that the conditions, including maintaining competence, have been met. A holder who misses the expiry date must apply for a new certificate and respond to a notice under section 155 of the WHS Act requiring evidence that they maintained competence and whether they practised after expiry.

The Regulator states plainly that practising in a statutory function with an expired certificate is an offense, and that failure to maintain the conditions of a certificate may result in suspension or cancellation.

blocks.text: The final row is an operator control rather than a scheme requirement. Operators that track certificate expiry in the same [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) as site inductions find gaps before an appointment lapses. For the wider WHS framework, see [the WHS Act duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training) and [high risk work licence requirements](/regulations/high-risk-work-licence-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each statutory function as a role linked to its learning groups, principal hazard topics and required hours, so learning delivered on site can be tagged to the group it counts toward. Mine operators can then see which appointees are short of hours in a group before renewal, rather than at audit. See the context for [energy and resources organizations](/industries/energy-resources).

faqs.q: Does in-house training count toward maintenance of competence?
faqs.a: It can. The Regulator's guidance lists participating in formal courses, seminars and workshops, self-directed learning, on-the-job training, and industry conferences and webinars as learning activities. Under the 2025 scheme, learning must meet the gazetted meaning of formal learning or be one of the listed informal types, and must be directly relevant to a learning group and the holder's function.

faqs.q: What if a holder has more than one statutory function?
faqs.a: Section 7.2 of the Regulator's guide says the holder must satisfy the function with the highest requirements, for one class of mine only. Where the functions are in different disciplines, such as electrical engineer and undermanager, the highest requirement in each discipline applies, although learning common to both disciplines can be claimed against each.

faqs.q: Can a NSW practising certificate be obtained through mutual recognition?
faqs.a: Yes. A person holding a current certificate to exercise an equivalent statutory function in another state or New Zealand can apply for mutual recognition, or use automatic mutual recognition for temporary registration except for Queensland certificates. The Regulator notes that South Australian and Victorian certificates of competence are no longer required in those states, so they cannot be recognized directly.

faqs.q: Was there any COVID-19 relief on learning hours?
faqs.a: Yes. The Regulator and the Mining and Petroleum Competence Board approved a 12 month dispensation equal to 20% of learning hours for holders who held a certificate between April 1, 2020 and March 31, 2021, so those holders need only complete 80% of the hours for that certificate period.

factCheck.claim: An individual must hold a current practising certificate to practise in a statutory function; certificates specify the function under Schedule 10 of the WHS (Mines and Petroleum Sites) Regulation 2022 and are issued for up to 5 years
Holding a practising certificate became mandatory from October 1, 2020 for statutory functions requiring one

Total learning hours over 5 years: 120 for mining, electrical and mechanical engineering managers, 90 for undermanagers and tier 1 quarry managers, 60 for deputies, open cut examiners, underground mine supervisors and any tier 2 quarry managers; groups 1 and 2 minimum 33%, group 3 maximum 33%
The scheme was developed in 2017 following inquiries into the Moura No. 2 and Pike River disasters

From October 1, 2025 up to 40% of hours may be claimed in one year, minimum formal learning proportions were removed, informal types expanded from 14 to 19, and 7 hours of formal disaster learning is mandatory for first-time holders
Audits are conducted randomly on an annual basis by external organizations, with outcomes reported to the NSW Mining and Petroleum Competence Board
Renewal can be applied for within 6 months of expiry; after expiry a new application and a WHS Act section 155 notice apply; practising with an expired certificate is an offense
